1	# Mise: build spec for a hands-free pantry-to-plate cooking app
2	
3	This SPEC.md specifies **Mise** (working name; rename freely), a Next.js web app built at HackCamp 2026 (nwPlus, UBC Vancouver, Nov 7–8, 2026). Users sign in with **Auth0**, add groceries by barcode, keep a per-user pantry with quantities and expiry dates in **Tiger Data** (TimescaleDB/Postgres), and get **real recipes found online by Gemini**, ranked toward whatever expires soonest. The original recipe is always shown first with attribution; an "AI-adapted" variant appears only when an ingredient is missing. Users cook hands-free with **MediaPipe** webcam gestures (scroll, next/previous step, timer, read aloud), with steps read aloud by **ElevenLabs** and `speechSynthesis` as the fallback. Finishing a recipe deducts what was used from the pantry and logs calories and protein in one database transaction. The app is served over HTTPS from a **Vultr** VPS, which the camera requires. The spec is written so three Claude Code accounts can build it in parallel through **Entire**. A Phase 0 foundation freezes the contracts in `src/contracts/`, the SQL schema and the stubs. After that, three workstreams (Cook Mode, Pantry & Nutrition, Recipes & Cooking Backend) each own separate directories, and an integration phase merges them. Researched facts are cited inline. Anything not confirmed against a primary source in research is marked **[VERIFY]**, and the open items are collected in §17. Treat those as the first things to check, not as settled.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 0. How to use this document
8	
9	- **Who reads this:** three Claude Code agents (one per teammate account) plus the humans steering them. Each agent reads §1–§8 (shared ground truth), its own workstream in §18, and the relevant feature sections in §9.
10	- **Source of truth order:** `src/contracts/**` (code) > this SPEC > comments. If the SPEC and the contracts disagree after Phase 0, the contracts win. Raise the mismatch with a human; don't silently diverge.
11	- **Markers:** **[VERIFY]** = not confirmed against a primary source during research; check before relying on it. **P0** = required for the demo, **P1** = should have, **P2** = stretch.
12	- Anthropic's guidance for specs like this: "The most useful specs are self-contained: they name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step." Keep CLAUDE.md short ([Claude Code best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices.md)). This spec follows both.
13	
14	---
15	
16	## 1. Overview, goals and non-goals
17	
18	### 1.1 Problem and pitch
19	
20	Home cooks waste food they forgot they had, and following a recipe on a phone or laptop with wet, floury hands is awkward. Screens dim and you lose your place. Mise closes the loop: **scan groceries → know what expires → cook a real recipe that uses it → touch nothing while cooking → pantry and nutrition update themselves.** HackCamp's challenge is to "identify a problem facing a community and build a solution that makes a meaningful difference". Judging covers Problem & User Research, Innovation, Technical Implementation, Design & UX, and Presentation ([HackCamp 2026 Devpost](https://hackcamp-2026.devpost.com/)).
21	
22	### 1.2 Goals (all confirmed by the team)
23	
24	| # | Goal | Priority |
25	|---|---|---|
26	| G1 | Web app: Next.js App Router + TypeScript, deployed on Vultr over HTTPS | P0 |
27	| G2 | Auth0 login. Every pantry item, recipe, session and meal belongs to one user | P0 |
28	| G3 | Tiger Data (TimescaleDB/Postgres) as the only database | P0 |
29	| G4 | Add groceries by barcode, scanned with the camera or typed. Lookup chain: **dataandapis.com → Open Food Facts → Gemini reads a product/label photo → manual form** | P0 |
30	| G5 | Expiry date from a photo of the printed date (Gemini reads it, user confirms) or typed in | P0 |
31	| G6 | Pantry tracks quantities and expiry dates, and deducts ingredients after cooking | P0 |
32	| G7 | Gemini finds **real recipes online**, shown **original-first with source attribution**, ranked to prefer items closest to expiry | P0 |
33	| G8 | Only when an ingredient is missing, AI may propose an adaptation, clearly marked **"AI-adapted"** and kept separate from the original | P0 |
34	| G9 | MediaPipe hand gestures: scroll up/down, next/previous step, start/pause step timer, read step aloud | P0 |
35	| G10 | Read aloud with ElevenLabs, falling back to browser `speechSynthesis` | P0 |
36	| G11 | Nutrition per pantry item and per recipe serving. Strict, code-enforced diet/allergy filters. Daily calorie and protein tracking | P0 |
37	| G12 | Meals logged through a "Finish cooking" prompt (servings eaten) and through manual logging | P0 |
38	| G13 | Built by 3 Claude Code accounts collaborating through Entire (Sessions, Graph, Brain, Trails) | P0 |
39	
40	### 1.3 Non-goals (explicitly out of scope)
41	
42	- Native mobile apps. PWA install/offline mode is also out (the site should still work in mobile browsers).
43	- Writing recipes from scratch with AI. The AI only *finds* recipes and *adapts* them when ingredients are missing.
44	- Medical or dietetic advice, or certified allergen guarantees. The app filters strictly but tells users to check labels.
45	- Shopping lists, grocery ordering, price tracking, meal planning calendars.
46	- Sharing pantries between users or households, and any social features.
47	- Contributing products back to Open Food Facts, which would need an OFF account for writes ([OFF API intro](https://openfoodfacts.github.io/openfoodfacts-server/api/)).
48	- Voice *commands* (speech recognition) are P2 only. The P0 hands-free channel is gestures plus read-aloud.
49	- Moving gesture inference to a Web Worker (P2; see §11.7).
50	- Hosted vector search or "similar recipes" (P2).
51	
52	### 1.4 Glossary
53	
54	- **Original recipe:** the recipe exactly as parsed from the publisher's page (schema.org `Recipe`), with attribution. Never modified.
55	- **AI-adapted recipe:** a separate object that references an original and lists explicit substitutions for missing ingredients.
56	- **Base units:** grams (mass), millilitres (volume), `count` (pieces). Every stored quantity uses one of them.
57	- **GTIN:** the canonical 13-digit (or 14-digit) barcode key. UPC-A is left-padded with `0`.
58	- **FEFO:** first-expired-first-out, the rule for choosing which pantry row to deduct from.
59	- **Armed:** the gesture state in which commands are accepted. Users arm it by holding an open palm.
60	
61	---
62	
63	## 2. User flows
64	
65	Each flow lists its happy path, then its branches. Feature IDs (F#) refer to §9.
66	
67	### UF1: Sign in and onboarding (F1)
68	1. A visitor lands on `/`. The marketing hero has a "Sign in" button that links to `/auth/login` (Auth0 Universal Login).
69	2. After callback, the first authenticated request upserts a `users` row keyed by Auth0 `sub`.
70	3. If `onboarded_at` is null, redirect to `/onboarding`. There the user sets diets (vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, dairy-free, high-protein), allergens, daily kcal and protein goals (optional), and time zone (default `America/Vancouver`).
71	4. The user lands on `/today`.
72	
73	### UF2: Add a grocery by barcode (F2, F4, F5)
74	1. `/pantry/add` opens the camera scanner, with the **"Type barcode" input always visible**.
75	2. A code is accepted after 2 identical consecutive reads and a valid check digit. The client calls `POST /api/products/lookup`.
76	3. **Found** (cache, dataandapis or OFF): show a confirmation card with name, brand, image, nutrition per 100 g, package size, and source attribution ("Data: Open Food Facts, ODbL").
77	4. The user sets quantity (pre-filled from package size when known) and unit, then sets expiry: **"Photo of date"** (UF4) or **"Enter date"** or "No date".
78	5. Save. The item appears in `/pantry`, sorted by soonest expiry.
79	- **Branch, not found:** "We couldn't find this product." → **"Take photo of product & nutrition label"** (UF3) → if that fails or is declined → **manual form**. The manual form is reachable from every step.
80	- **Branch, provider down** (401/402/429/5xx/timeout): treated as a miss for the user, logged server-side. The flow continues to OFF, then to the photo step.
81	
82	### UF3: Product from a label photo (F3)
83	1. The user captures 1–3 photos (front, nutrition panel, optional side). The client downscales them to about 1600 px on the long edge, JPEG q≈0.85.
84	2. `POST /api/vision/label` → Gemini returns a draft and the server runs sanity checks.
85	3. The manual form opens **pre-filled**. Flagged fields are highlighted. The user must press **Confirm** before anything is saved (`userVerified=true`).
86	
87	### UF4: Expiry date from a photo (F4)
88	1. The user takes a close photo of the printed date.
89	2. `POST /api/vision/expiry` → the server assembles a date from Gemini's components and cross-checks it with a CFIA regex.
90	3. A date picker opens pre-filled, with the raw text shown ("Read: `BB/MA 2026 NO 15`"). If the order is ambiguous, the user picks from the candidates. **The user must confirm.** "Packaged on" dates are never accepted as expiry; instead the UI says "This looks like a packaged-on date".
91	
92	### UF5: Find recipes (F6, F7, F10)
93	1. `/recipes` shows chips for expiring-soon items (≤ 3 days, pre-selected) and a "Find recipes" button. The user's diet/allergy filters appear as locked chips with a link to Settings.
94	2. `POST /api/recipes/search` streams progress ("Searching the web… / Reading 8 recipe pages… / Checking your allergies…"), then candidate cards arrive one by one.
95	3. Each card shows the title, the **source site and author**, coverage ("You have 7 of 9 ingredients"), the expiring items it uses (badge "uses spinach, expires in 2 days"), missing-ingredient count, ≈kcal and protein per serving, and total time.
96	4. Candidates that break a diet or allergy filter never appear. A collapsed "N recipes hidden by your filters" note lists them by reason (no recipe content shown).
97	
98	### UF6: Recipe detail, original first, optional adaptation (F8, F9, F10)
99	1. `/recipes/[recipeId]` shows the **Original** card first: title, "From {siteName} by {author}", a "View original" link, ingredients exactly as published (each marked have / missing / staple), steps, and nutrition (our estimate with coverage, plus "Publisher's nutrition" if the page provided it).
100	2. If the recipe has missing ingredients, a secondary button reads **"Suggest an AI adaptation using my pantry"**. Pressing it calls `POST /api/recipes/[id]/adapt`. The result appears in a **separate card with an "AI-adapted" badge** on a different background. It lists substitutions ("Missing: buttermilk → Using: Greek yogurt + lemon (from your pantry)"), changed steps, warnings, and re-estimated nutrition.
101	3. "Cook original" and "Cook AI-adapted" (when present) are separate buttons, each with a servings stepper.
102	
103	### UF7: Cook hands-free (F11, F12, F13)
104	1. "Cook" → `POST /api/cook/sessions` → `/cook/[sessionId]`. The **"Start cooking" tap** unlocks audio and requests a screen wake lock.
105	2. One step per screen, in large type. The step's ingredients and quantities are listed and timer chips are docked at the bottom.
106	3. A **"Hands-free" toggle** loads MediaPipe lazily, asks for camera permission, and shows the HUD with a gesture legend. Open palm (hold) arms the system. Then swipe = next/previous, thumb up/down (hold) = scroll, fist (hold) = timer start/pause, victory sign (hold) = read step aloud / stop.
107	4. Each control also has big tap targets and keyboard shortcuts.
108	5. Refreshing or reopening the page offers "Resume at step 5?". Timers continue correctly because they are stored as absolute end times.
109	
110	### UF8: Finish cooking (F14)
111	1. On the last step (or any time from the menu) → **"Finish cooking"** dialog.
112	2. The dialog shows **Servings cooked** (default = planned), **Servings you ate** (default 1; 0 allowed), and a **deduction preview** with one line per matched pantry item ("Spinach: 150 g of 200 g → 50 g left"). Lines are editable and can be unchecked. Lines the app couldn't convert are flagged "Adjust manually". The nutrition for the servings eaten is editable.
113	3. Confirm → one transaction deducts the pantry, writes pantry events, inserts the meal log and closes the session → navigate to `/today` with a toast ("Logged 1 serving · 540 kcal · 32 g protein").
114	
115	### UF9: Daily tracking and manual logging (F15)
116	1. `/today` shows kcal and protein rings against the goals, today's meals list, a 7-day bar chart, and "Expiring soon" pantry items.
117	2. **"Log food"** offers three tabs: *From pantry* (pick item + amount; "Also remove from pantry" checkbox, default on), *Scan* (barcode → product → amount), *Quick add* (label + kcal + protein).
118	3. The user can delete a meal from today's list.

164	Key properties:

254	## 5. Data model (Tiger Data / TimescaleDB)
255	
256	### 5.1 Design rules
257	
258	- **Base units everywhere.** Store `quantity_base` in g, ml or count, and keep the user's `display_unit` alongside for display.
259	- **Nutrition per 100 g or 100 ml** is canonical. Per serving is derived, or stored when the source gives it.
260	- **Mutable state goes in plain tables:** `pantry_items`, `recipes`, `recipe_variants`, `cooking_sessions`.
261	- **Append-only, time-keyed data goes in hypertables:** `meal_logs`, `pantry_events`. A continuous aggregate `daily_nutrition` provides history charts.
262	- Hypertable constraints: unique indexes must include the partitioning column, and hypertable-to-hypertable foreign keys are unsupported ([Tiger limitations](https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/deploy/limitations/index.md); [primary keys](https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/learn/data-model/primary-keys-time-and-uniqueness)). Hence `PRIMARY KEY (id, eaten_at)`, and nothing references `meal_logs`.
263	- Hypertable syntax `WITH (tsdb.hypertable, tsdb.partition_column = '…')` and the continuous-aggregate and policy syntax come from [Tiger's continuous aggregate docs](https://tigerdata.com/docs/build/continuous-aggregates/create-a-continuous-aggregate). Continuous-aggregate `GROUP BY` must include `time_bucket` on the time column, and the source hypertable cannot use row-level security. That is fine here, because isolation is enforced in application code.
264	- **Nutrition in `meal_logs` is a snapshot.** Later recipe edits never rewrite history.
265	- **Every query is scoped by `user_id`**, which comes from `requireUser()` and never from the request body.

470	SELECT add_continuous_aggregate_policy('daily_nutrition',

1691	## 12. UX rules (apply everywhere)
1692	
1693	1. **Original before AI, always.** Anything Gemini *generated or transformed* carries a visible badge: "AI-adapted" on adaptations, "Read by AI, please confirm" on label and expiry drafts, "≈ estimate" on computed nutrition. Publisher content carries attribution instead.
1694	2. **Confirm before save** for every AI extraction. Nothing from Gemini reaches the database without a user tap.
1695	3. **Every gesture has a tap and a keyboard equivalent.** Gestures are never the only path, and hands-free is opt-in per session.
1696	4. **Kitchen-distance readability in cook mode:**
1697	   - Step text ≥ 32 px.
1698	   - One step per screen.
1699	   - Tap targets ≥ 25% of width for Prev and Next, and ≥ 56 px elsewhere.
1700	   - Contrast ≥ WCAG AA. Dark theme default in cook mode.
1701	5. **Colour is never the only signal.** Expiry bands also show text ("2 days"), and have/missing markers use icon + label.
1702	6. **Feedback for hands-free actions** goes through three channels: visual flash, sound, and `aria-live` text. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
1703	7. **Progressive results.** Recipe search streams status messages and cards. Never show a spinner with no message for more than 2 s.
1704	8. **Honest empty and error states:**
1705	   - "We couldn't find this product" leads straight to the next fallback.
1706	   - "Camera blocked" offers buttons and keyboard.
1707	   - "Voice: Device" appears when ElevenLabs is unavailable.
1708	9. **"Best before", not "Expires"**, unless Gemini classified the date as `expiry`/`use_by`. Show the raw printed text next to the parsed date.
1709	10. **Allergy copy:** filters are strict, but the app always says "Always check product labels for allergens." Never claim a recipe is "safe".
1710	11. **Units:** show the user's display unit and accept common abbreviations. Never show raw base units to users.
1711	12. **Design deliverable:** produce a Figma file of the main screens (Today, Pantry, Scan, Recipes, Recipe detail with Original + AI-adapted, Cook mode + HUD) for the Best Design submission (§16).

1715	## 13. Security and privacy
1716	
1717	| Area | Rule |
1718	|---|---|
1719	| Secrets | Server-only. None use the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix. `.env.production` lives on the VPS with `chmod 600` and is never baked into the image. Entire's secrets redaction is a bonus, not a control |
1720	| AuthZ | `requireUser()` in every route handler and Server Action. Every SQL statement includes `user_id = ${user.id}`. IDs in URLs are always re-checked against the user, and a mismatch returns **404** (not 403) |
1721	| Input validation | Zod on every body and query. Barcode digits 8–14. Text caps (TTS 2000, freeText 100). Image MIME allowlist and ≤ 4 MB each, ≤ 3 per request |
1722	| LLM output | Treated as untrusted input: Zod-validated, values sanity-checked, pantry IDs verified, allergens re-checked in code, URLs verified by fetch |
1723	| SSRF (recipe fetcher) | `server/recipes/safe-fetch.ts`: only `http(s)` on ports 80/443. Resolve DNS and **reject private, loopback, link-local and metadata IPs** (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 127/8, 169.254/16, ::1, fc00::/7), re-checked on every redirect. Max 5 redirects, 5 s timeout, 2 MB body cap, `text/html` only |
1724	| Rendering third-party HTML | Never `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` publisher HTML. Parse it to text. Gemini's Search Suggestions HTML is rendered **unmodified inside a sandboxed `<iframe srcdoc>`** (`sandbox="allow-popups allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox"`) **[VERIFY this satisfies the Grounding display terms]** |
1725	| Camera and video | Frames are processed locally and never recorded, uploaded or stored. Model and WASM are self-hosted, so there are no third-party requests while hands-free is on. The camera starts only after an explicit toggle, a persistent indicator is shown, and tracks stop on toggle-off, page hide and route leave |
1726	| Photos | Label and expiry photos go to Gemini through our server for one request and are **not persisted** (memory only). The UI copy says so |
1727	| Headers | `Permissions-Policy: camera=(self), microphone=()`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`. CSP (P1): `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'`; `img-src 'self' data: blob: https:`; `media-src 'self' blob:`; `connect-src 'self'`; `worker-src 'self' blob:`. The `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` source is needed for Emscripten WASM (general knowledge **[VERIFY]**) |
1728	| Abuse and cost | Per-user rate limits (§7). TTS text cap. Discovery cache. Barcode cache and single-flight |
1729	| Licensing and attribution | "Product data © Open Food Facts contributors, ODbL" in the footer and on product cards. OFF images are CC BY-SA. Recipe attribution and "View original" on every recipe |
1730	| Data deletion | Settings → "Delete my data" deletes the `users` row (cascades) (P1) |

2011	  1. The agent stops and asks its human.
2012	  2. The human makes **one small dedicated commit** on `main` titled `contract: …`. It is additive whenever possible: new optional fields, new routes, a new migration file `0003_*.sql` rather than editing old ones.
2013	  3. The human announces it in team chat and runs `entire brain remember "…"`.
2014	  4. All workstreams rebase.
2015	- **`package.json`:** request the dependency in team chat. One designated person (the Phase 0 owner) adds it with an exact version and pushes. Never edit the lockfile in parallel.
2016	- **Optional enforcement:** a Claude Code `PreToolUse` hook (`.claude/hooks/guard-paths.mjs`) that reads the edited `file_path` from the hook input and blocks (exit code 2) any path outside the allowlist for `$MISE_WS` (A/B/C), as well as any path under `src/contracts/**`. Anthropic recommends hooks for "actions that must happen every time with zero exceptions" ([best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices.md)). **[VERIFY hook input format in the Claude Code hooks docs.]**
2017	
2018	### 18.6 Entire setup and usage (every teammate)
2019	
2020	```bash
2021	curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash      # entire.io now redirects to entire.com
2022	entire login
2023	cd mise && entire enable --agent claude-code

2029	
2030	Sources: [entireio/cli](https://github.com/entireio/cli); [Brain docs](https://docs.entire.com/guides/brain/overview.md). Brain requires **Claude Code 2.1.78+**, has no `entire brain mcp` command, and keeps memories local until you connect. Commit `.entire/agent-guide.md` and the managed `CLAUDE.md` block. Do **not** use the stale `npm install -g @entireio/cli` / `entire init` / `entire capture` commands found in older third-party write-ups.
2031	
2032	How each Entire capability gets used, which doubles as prize proof:
2033	- **Sessions:** automatic. Every Claude Code session is captured. On commit, an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer is added and metadata goes to `entire/checkpoints/v1`, with no extra commits on your branch ([entireio/cli](https://github.com/entireio/cli); [Sessions](https://docs.entire.com/guides/sessions/overview.md)). Use `entire session resume` to pick up work, and `entire checkpoint explain <id>` in reviews.
2034	- **Graph:** a code map that agents query for "what does changing `RecipeStep` affect?". Entire claims "up to 71%" token savings, without giving a method ([Graph overview](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/overview.md)).
2035	- **Brain:** **each agent starts every session with `entire brain brief "<task>" --json`**. Record decisions with `entire brain remember` (e.g. "swipe right→left = next", "finish route returns 409 on replay"). Show `entire brain recall`, `viz` and `dash` in the demo.
2036	- **Trails:** one per workstream, created in Phase 0 with `entire trail create --title "Cook Mode: gestures + voice" --no-branch` and then linked to the branch with `entire trail link`. Eval scores (e.g. Security, Slop) are "calculated on every push", so push often for a visible history ([Trails](https://docs.entire.com/guides/trails/overview.md)). Run `entire agent-help` so agents can create and update trails themselves.
2037	- **Labs (verify availability with `entire labs`):** `entire blame <file>` and `entire why <file>:<line>`. Demo these on the gesture threshold constants and the allergen map.
2038	- `/session handoff` was **not found** in the docs. Don't rely on it (§17 item 13).
2039	
2040	---
2041	
2042	## 19. Suggested CLAUDE.md (commit at repo root; keep it this short)
2043	
2044	Anthropic advises: "Keep it concise. For each line, ask: 'Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?'" Include commands, gotchas and repository etiquette, and exclude file-by-file tours ([best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices.md)).
2045	
2046	```markdown
2047	# Mise — agent rules
2048	
2049	Spec: @SPEC.md (contracts in src/contracts/ win over prose). Tasks: @TASKS.md
2050	
2051	## Commands
2052	- npm run dev | npm run build | npm run typecheck | npm run lint | npm test | npm run test:db
2053	- Migrations: node scripts/migrate.mjs  (never edit an applied migration; add 000N_*.sql)
2054	- Definition of done for any task: typecheck + lint + test green, and the feature's ACs in SPEC §9.
2055	
2056	## Ownership (do NOT edit outside your workstream; ask your human instead)
2057	- WS-A Cook Mode: src/features/{gesture,cook,voice}, src/app/(app)/cook, src/app/api/tts, public/{mediapipe,models}
2058	- WS-B Pantry/Nutrition: src/features/{scan,pantry,nutrition}, src/server/{products,vision,pantry}, src/server/nutrition/daily*, app pages onboarding/settings/today/pantry, api me/products/vision/pantry/meals/nutrition
2059	- WS-C Recipes/Cook backend: src/features/recipes, src/server/{recipes,diet,cook}, src/server/nutrition/recipe*, app pages recipes, api recipes/cook
2060	- FROZEN (Phase 0; change only via a human "contract:" commit): src/contracts/**, src/lib/**, src/components/ui/**, db/migrations/0001-0002, package.json, layout/globals, Docker/Caddy files
2061	
2062	## Hard rules
2063	- Every route handler / Server Action starts with `const user = await requireUser()`; every SQL filters by user.id. Never read userId from the request.
2064	- Secrets are server-only; never prefix with NEXT_PUBLIC_. Never log API keys or photos.
2065	- All Gemini calls go through src/lib/gemini (geminiJson / geminiGroundedSearch). Never combine googleSearch tool with a response schema.
2066	- LLM output is untrusted: zod-validate, re-check allergens with server/diet/checkDiet, verify pantry IDs and URLs.
2067	- Show the ORIGINAL recipe verbatim with attribution; AI-adapted content is a separate variant with an "AI-adapted" badge. Never mutate an original variant.
2068	- Store quantities in base units (g/ml/count) via src/lib/units; never guess cross-dimension conversions.
2069	- MediaPipe/camera code: 'use client', loaded via next/dynamic({ssr:false}) from a client component; full cleanup in useEffect; never @latest URLs; frames never leave the device.
2070	- Timers use absolute endsAt timestamps, never decrementing counters.
2071	- Pin exact dependency versions; ask the human before adding a dependency.
2072	
2073	## Workflow
2074	- Start each session: `entire brain brief "<your task>" --json`. Record decisions: `entire brain remember "<decision>"`.
2075	- Small commits (each = Entire checkpoint). Conventional prefix: feat(ws-a): / fix(ws-c): / test: / contract:
2076	- Rebase on main often. Run /code-review in a fresh session before merging.
2077	- Mark [VERIFY] items you resolve in SPEC §17 via your human.
2078	```
2079	
2080	---
2081	
2082	## Conclusion
2083	
2084	The riskiest parts of this build aren't gestures or auth. They are three LLM boundaries: finding real URLs, reading labels and dates, and adapting recipes. In each one, Gemini's output can be well-formed and still wrong. The spec therefore keeps Gemini out of every decision that has to be correct. Gemini finds candidate URLs, but the recipe content shown is whatever the publisher's own markup says, fetched and parsed by our code. Gemini reads a label, but a person confirms it. Gemini proposes a substitution, and `checkDiet` decides whether it is allowed. That split is also what lets three agents work in parallel safely, because the deterministic modules (units, GTIN, diet, scoring, timers, the gesture engine) are pure and testable against frozen contracts with no network. The two choices most worth revisiting after the event are the gesture thresholds in §11.4, which no published study validates, and how much publisher step text to store. That second one is a product and legal call, and the research could only partly settle it.
2085

## Your setup tasks while Jerry scaffolds

**1. Auth0** (manage.auth0.com)
- Create a tenant. Then go to Applications → Create Application → **Regular Web Application**.
- In the app's Settings, set:
  - Allowed Callback URLs: `http://localhost:3000/auth/callback`
  - Allowed Logout URLs: `http://localhost:3000`
  - Allowed Web Origins: `http://localhost:3000`
  - Add the `https://<domain>` versions once Hang gives you the production URL.
- Under Authentication → Social, enable **Google**.
- Save the Domain, Client ID and Client Secret.
- Generate `AUTH0_SECRET` in Git Bash with `openssl rand -hex 32`.

**2. Tiger Data** (console.cloud.timescale.com)
- Create a free service named `mise-db` with TimescaleDB (not plain Postgres), region `us-east-1`.
- **Download the config right away.** It's the only time the password is shown.
- Fork that service and name the fork `mise-test`.
- Save both connection strings. They become `DATABASE_URL` and `DATABASE_URL_TEST`.

**3. dataandapis.com**
- Sign up for Barcode Lookup and save the API key (`DATAANDAPIS_KEY`).
- Note which plan it's on. Free is 500 tokens/month, which matters for §17 item 4.

**4. Entire:** run `! entire auth status` and fix access to `gh/nougify` so trails and `entire review` work.

Keep the secrets in a password manager for now. Don't create `.env.local` until the scaffold's `.gitignore` is on main. After that, put them in `.env.local` and never `git add` it.

# AGENTS.md **SDK:** `@auth0/nextjs-auth0` **Purpose:** Auth0 authentication for Next.js (App Router + Pages Router) **Runtime:** Node 20+, ESM, TypeScript > **Agent skills:** for task-specific, version-pinned guidance read > [`skills/SKILL.md`](skills/SKILL.md) (hub) and its sub-skills > (e.g. `skills/mfa/SKILL.md`). These ship inside the published package, so > they are also present under `node_modules/@auth0/nextjs-auth0/skills/` in a consuming app. --- ## Quick Commands | Task | Command | |------|---------| | Install | `pnpm install` | | Build | `pnpm run build` | | Test unit | `pnpm test:unit` | | Test e2e | `pnpm test:e2e` | | Lint + typecheck | `pnpm run lint` | | Generate docs | `pnpm run docs` | --- ## Package Exports | Import Path | Contents | |-------------|----------| | `@auth0/nextjs-auth0` | Client: `useUser`, `getAccessToken`, `Auth0Provider`, `withPageAuthRequired` | | `@auth0/nextjs-auth0/server` | Server: `Auth0Client`, `AbstractSessionStore`, `TransactionStore` | | `@auth0/nextjs-auth0/errors` | Error classes: `SdkError`, `AccessTokenError`, `AuthorizationError`, etc. | | `@auth0/nextjs-auth0/types` | TypeScript types only: `SessionData`, `User`, `TokenSet` | | `@auth0/nextjs-auth0/testing` | Test utilities: `generateSessionCookie` | --- ## Architecture ``` src/ ├── client/ # React hooks, Auth0Provider, client getAccessToken │ ├── hooks/ # useUser │ ├── helpers/ # getAccessToken, withPageAuthRequired │ └── providers/ # Auth0Provider ├── server/ # Auth0Client (public API), AuthClient (internal) │ ├── session/ # Stateless (cookie) + Stateful (external store) │ ├── helpers/ # withPageAuthRequired, withApiAuthRequired │ ├── client.ts # Auth0Client - main public class │ └── auth-client.ts # Internal route handling + OAuth flows ├── errors/ # SdkError hierarchy (catch by error.code) ├── types/ # SessionData, User, TokenSet, AuthorizationParameters ├── utils/ # Internal: dpop, paths, scopes, urls └── testing/ # generateSessionCookie for test session setup ``` --- ## Data Flows Legend: `→` flow, `↔` bidirectional, `[]` storage, `{}` transform | Flow | Path | |------|------| | Login | Browser→`/auth/login`→Auth0`/authorize`→`/auth/callback`→{tokenSet}→[session cookie]→redirect | | Logout | Browser→`/auth/logout`→[clear session]→Auth0`/oidc/logout`→redirect | | getSession | [cookie]→{decrypt}→SessionData | | getAccessToken | [session]→?expired→Auth0`/oauth/token`→{refresh}→[session update]→token | | getAccessToken (client) | Browser→`/auth/access-token`→[session]→token | | useUser | Browser→`/auth/profile`→[session]→User | | Stateful session | [cookie:sid]↔[external store:SessionData] | See [EXAMPLES.md](EXAMPLES.md) for detailed flow implementations. --- ## Key Patterns ### Public API Surface | Class/Function | Location | Purpose | |----------------|----------|---------| | `Auth0Client` | `./server` | Main SDK entry, instantiate once per app | | `useUser()` | `./client` | React hook for authenticated user | | `getAccessToken()` | `./client` | Client-side token retrieval | | `Auth0Provider` | `./client` | Context provider wrapping app | | `withPageAuthRequired` | `./client` or `./server` | Page protection HOC | ### Session Storage | Mode | Implementation | When | |------|----------------|------| | Stateless (default) | Encrypted cookie | No external deps | | Stateful | Custom `SessionDataStore` | Large sessions, server-side revocation | ### Multi-Resource Refresh Tokens (MRRT) - Multiple access tokens stored per audience in `session.accessTokens[]` - Automatic token refresh per audience ### DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession) - Optional, requires `dpop.enabled: true` + key pair config - Tokens bound to cryptographic proof ### Hooks | Hook | Trigger | |------|---------| | `beforeSessionSaved` | Before session persisted, modify session data | | `onCallback` | After OAuth callback, customize redirect/session | --- ## Error Handling Base class: `SdkError` with `code: string` property. | Error Class | Code | Cause | |-------------|------|-------| | `AccessTokenError` | `access_token_error` | Token fetch/refresh failure | | `AuthorizationError` | `authorization_error` | OAuth authorize failure | | `InvalidConfigurationError` | `invalid_configuration` | Bad SDK config | | `DiscoveryError` | `discovery_error` | OIDC discovery failed | | `OAuth2Error` | varies | Auth0 callback error (may contain user input) | **Pattern:** Catch by `error.code`, not `instanceof`. --- ## Environment Variables ### Required | Variable | Purpose | |----------|---------| | `AUTH0_DOMAIN` | Auth0 tenant domain | | `AUTH0_CLIENT_ID` | Application client ID | | `AUTH0_CLIENT_SECRET` | Application client secret | | `AUTH0_SECRET` | Session encryption key (min 32 chars) | | `APP_BASE_URL` | Application base URL | ### Optional | Variable | Purpose | |----------|---------| | `AUTH0_COOKIE_*` | Cookie configuration overrides | | `AUTH0_DPOP_*` | DPoP configuration | | `NEXT_PUBLIC_*_ROUTE` | Custom route paths | --- ## Testing ### Unit Tests - Install the SDK ```shell npm i @auth0/nextjs-auth0 ``` This library requires Node.js 20 LTS and newer LTS versions. ### 2. Add the environment variables Add the following environment variables to your `.env.local` file: ```env AUTH0_DOMAIN= AUTH0_CLIENT_ID= AUTH0_CLIENT_SECRET= AUTH0_SECRET= APP_BASE_URL= # optional for dynamic preview environments ``` The `AUTH0_DOMAIN`, `AUTH0_CLIENT_ID`, and `AUTH0_CLIENT_SECRET` can be obtained from the [Auth0 Dashboard](https://manage.auth0.com) once you've created an application. **This application must be a `Regular Web Application`**. The `AUTH0_SECRET` is the key used to encrypt the session and transaction cookies. You can generate a secret using `openssl`: ```shell openssl rand -hex 32 ``` The `APP_BASE_URL` is the URL that your application is running on. When developing locally, this is most commonly `http://localhost:3000`. If you omit it, the SDK will infer the base URL from the incoming request host at runtime. > [!IMPORTANT] > You will need to register the following URLs in your Auth0 Application via the [Auth0 Dashboard](https://manage.auth0.com): > > - Add `http://localhost:3000/auth/callback` to the list of **Allowed Callback URLs** > - Add `http://localhost:3000` to the list of **Allowed Logout URLs** > > When using dynamic hosts (preview environments), ensure the resulting callback and logout URLs are registered in your Auth0 application. #### Dynamic base URLs (Preview deployments) For preview environments (`Vercel`, `Netlify`), you can omit `APP_BASE_URL` and let the SDK infer the base URL from the incoming request host at runtime. This keeps dynamic preview URLs working without extra configuration. If you know the base URL at startup (for example, a stable production domain), set `appBaseUrl` or `APP_BASE_URL` to a single absolute URL. Comma-separated values are not supported. Because the Host header is untrusted input, Auth0's Allowed Callback URLs are the safety net in this mode: if the inferred host is not registered, Auth0 rejects the authorize request. Example (dynamic): ```ts import { Auth0Client } from "@auth0/nextjs-auth0/server"; export const auth0 = new Auth0Client(); ``` Example (static): ```ts import { Auth0Client } from "@auth0/nextjs-auth0/server"; export const auth0 = new Auth0Client({ appBaseUrl: "https://app.example.com" }); ``` > [!NOTE] > When relying on dynamic base URLs in production, the SDK enforces secure cookies. If you explicitly set `AUTH0_COOKIE_SECURE=false`, `session.cookie.secure=false`, or `transactionCookie.secure=false`, the SDK throws `InvalidConfigurationError`. ### 3. Create the Auth0 SDK client Create an instance of the Auth0 client. This instance will be imported and used in anywhere you need access to the authentication methods on the server. Add the following contents to a file named `lib/auth0.ts`: ```ts import { Auth0Client } from "@auth0/nextjs-auth0/server"; export const auth0 = new Auth0Client(); ``` > [!NOTE] > The Auth0Client automatically uses safe defaults to manage authentication cookies. For advanced use cases, you can customize transaction cookie behavior by providing your own configuration. See [Transaction Cookie Configuration](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#transaction-cookie-configuration) for details. ### 4. Add the authentication middleware Authentication requests in Next.js are intercepted at the network boundary using a middleware or proxy file. Follow the setup below depending on your Next.js version. #### 🟦 On Next.js 15 Create a `middleware.ts` file in the root of your project: ```ts import type { NextRequest } from "next/server"; import { auth0 } from "./lib/auth0"; // Adjust path if your auth0 client is elsewhere export async function middleware(request: NextRequest) { return await auth0.middleware(request); } export const config = { matcher: [ /* * Match all request paths except for: * - _next/static (static files) * - _next/image (image optimization files) * - favicon.ico, sitemap.xml, robots.txt (metadata files) */ "/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)" ] }; ``` > [!NOTE] > If you're using a `src/` directory, the `middleware.ts` file must be created inside the `src/` directory. #### 🟨 On Next.js 16 Next.js 16 introduces a new convention called proxy.ts, replacing middleware.ts. This change better represents the network interception boundary and unifies request handling for both the Edge and Node runtimes. Create a proxy.ts file in the root of your project (Or rename your existing middleware.ts to proxy.ts): ```ts import { auth0 } from "./lib/auth0"; export async function proxy(request: Request) { // Note that proxy uses the standard Request type return await auth0.middleware(request); } export const config = { matcher: [ "/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)" ] }; ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > Starting with **Next.js 16**, the recommended file for handling authentication boundaries is **`proxy.ts`**. You can still continue using **`middleware.ts`** for backward compatibility, it will work under the **Edge runtime** in Next.js 16. However, it is **deprecated** for the Node runtime and will be removed in a future release. > > The new proxy layer also executes slightly earlier in the routing pipeline, so make sure your matcher patterns do not conflict with other proxy or middleware routes. > > Additionally, the Edge runtime now applies stricter header and cookie validation, > so avoid setting non-string cookie values or invalid header formats. > [!IMPORTANT] > This broad middleware matcher is essential for rolling sessions and security features. For scenarios when rolling sessions are disabled, see [Session Configuration](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#session-configuration) for alternative approaches. You can now begin to authenticate your users by redirecting them to your application's `/auth/login` route: ```tsx import { auth0 } from "./lib/auth0"; // Adjust path if your auth0 client is elsewhere export default async function Home() { const session = await auth0.getSession(); if (!session) { return (
Sign up Log in
); } return (

Welcome, {session.user.name}!

); } ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > A default `` is safe — the SDK detects the AUTO prefetch header and returns `204 No Content` without writing a transaction cookie. Avoid `` (FULL prefetch): it sends no detectable prefetch header, so the SDK cannot distinguish it from a real navigation and will start a login flow. Use a plain `` tag or `` if you need to be safe across all prefetch modes. See [Preventing "431 Request Header Fields Too Large" Errors](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#preventing-431-request-header-fields-too-large-errors) for details. ## Customizing the client You can customize the client by using the options below: | Option | Type | Description | | --------------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | domain | `string \| DomainResolver` | The Auth0 domain for the tenant (e.g.: `example.us.auth0.com`). Accepts a static string or a `DomainResolver` function for [Multiple Custom Domains](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#multiple-custom-domains-mcd). Falls back to `AUTH0_DOMAIN` environment variable. | | clientId | `string` | The Auth0 client ID. If it's not specified, it will be loaded from the `AUTH0_CLIENT_ID` environment variable. | | clientSecret | `string` | The Auth0 client secret. If it's not specified, it will be loaded from the `AUTH0_CLIENT_SECRET` environment variable. | | authorizationParameters | `AuthorizationParameters` | The authorization parameters to pass to the `/authorize` endpoint. See [Passing authorization parameters](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#passing-authorization-parameters) for more details. | | clientAssertionSigningKey | `string` or `CryptoKey` | Private key for use with `private_key_jwt` clients. This can also be specified via the `AUTH0_CLIENT_ASSERTION_SIGNING_KEY` environment variable. | | clientAssertionSigningAlg | `string` | The algorithm used to sign the client assertion JWT. This can also be provided via the `AUTH0_CLIENT_ASSERTION_SIGNING_ALG` environment variable. | | appBaseUrl | `string` | The URL of your application (e.g.: `http://localhost:3000`). If it's not specified, it will be loaded from the `APP_BASE_URL` environment variable or inferred from the request host at runtime. | | logoutStrategy | `"auto" \| "oidc" \| "v2"` | Strategy for logout endpoint selection. `"auto"` (default) uses OIDC logout when available, falls back to `/v2/logout`. `"oidc"` always uses OIDC logout. `"v2"` always uses `/v2/logout` endpoint which supports wildcard URLs. See [Configuring logout strategy](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#configuring-logout-strategy) for details. | | includeIdTokenHintInOIDCLogoutUrl | `boolean` | Configure whether to include `id_token_hint` in OIDC logout URLs for privacy. Defaults to `true` (recommended). When `false`, excludes PII from logout URLs but reduces DoS protection. See [OIDC logout privacy configuration](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#oidc-logout-privacy-configuration) for details. | | secret | `string` | A 32-byte, hex-encoded secret used for encrypting cookies. If it's not specified, it will be loaded from the `AUTH0_SECRET` environment variable. | | signInReturnToPath | `string` | The path to redirect the user to after successfully authenticating. Defaults to `/`. | | session | `SessionConfiguration` | Configure the session timeouts and whether to use rolling sessions or not, including a `beforeSessionRolled` predicate to selectively roll the session per request. See [Session configuration](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#session-configuration) and [Selectively rolling sessions](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#selectively-rolling-sessions) for additional details. Also allows configuration of cookie attributes like `domain`, `path`, `secure`, `sameSite`, and `transient`. If not specified, these can be configured using `AUTH0_COOKIE_*` environment variables. Note: `httpOnly` is always `true`. See [Cookie Configuration](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#cookie-configuration) for details. | | enableParallelTransactions | `boolean` | Enable support for multiple concurrent authentication flows by using unique transaction cookies per flow. When `true` (default), each authentication attempt gets its own transaction cookie with a unique state suffix. When `false`, uses a single shared transaction cookie, which may cause conflicts with concurrent auth attempts. See [Transaction Cookie Configuration](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#transaction-cookie-configuration) for details. | | transactionCookie | `TransactionCookieOptions` | Configure transaction cookie management for authentication flows. You can control cookie expiration and other cookie options. See [Transaction Cookie Configuration](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#transaction-cookie-configuration) for details. | | beforeSessionSaved | `BeforeSessionSavedHook` | A method to manipulate the session before persisting it. See [beforeSessionSaved](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#beforesessionsaved) for additional details. | | onCallback | `OnCallbackHook` | A method to handle errors or manage redirects after attempting to authenticate. See [onCallback](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#oncallback) for additional details. | | sessionStore | `SessionStore` | A custom session store implementation used to persist sessions to a data store. See [Database sessions](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#database-sessions) for additional details. | | pushedAuthorizationRequests | `boolean` | Configure the SDK to use the Pushed Authorization Requests (PAR) protocol when communicating with the authorization server. | | routes | `Routes` | Configure the paths for the authentication routes. See [Custom routes](https://github.com/auth0/nextjs-auth0/blob/main/EXAMPLES.md#custom-routes) for additional details. | | allowInsecureRequests | `boolean` | Allow insecure requests to be made to the authorization server. This can be useful when testing with a mock OIDC provider that does not support TLS, locally. This option can only be used when `NODE_ENV` is not set to `production`. | | httpTimeout | `number` | Integer value for the HTTP timeout in milliseconds for authentication requests. Defaults to `5000` milliseconds | | enableTelemetry | `boolean` | Boolean value to opt-out of sending the library name and version to your authorization server via the `Auth0-Client` header. 10	
11	> **Note**: The `middleware` file convention is deprecated and has been renamed to `proxy`. See [Migration to Proxy](#migration-to-proxy) for more details.
12	
13	The `proxy.js|ts` file is used to write [Proxy](/docs/app/getting-started/proxy) and run code on the server before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.
14	
15	Proxy executes before routes are rendered. It's particularly useful for implementing custom server-side logic like authentication, logging, or handling redirects.
16	
17	> **Good to know**:
18	>
19	> Proxy is meant to be invoked separately of your render code and in optimized cases deployed to your CDN for fast redirect/rewrite handling, you should not attempt relying on shared modules or globals.
20	>
21	> To pass information from Proxy to your application, use [headers](#setting-headers), [cookies](#using-cookies), [rewrites](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#rewrite), [redirects](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#redirect), or the URL.
22	
23	Create a `proxy.ts` (or `.js`) file in the project root, or inside `src` if applicable, so that it is located at the same level as `pages` or `app`.
24	
25	If you’ve customized [`pageExtensions`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/pageExtensions), for example to `.page.ts` or `.page.js`, name your file `proxy.page.ts` or `proxy.page.js` accordingly.
26

29	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
30	
31	// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
32	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
33	  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
34	}
35	
36	export const config = {
37	  matcher: '/about/:path*',
38	}
39	```

54	## Exports
55	
56	### Proxy function
57	
58	The file must export a single function, either as a default export or named `proxy`. Note that multiple proxy from the same file are not supported.
59	
60	```js filename="proxy.js"
61	// Example of default export
62	export default function proxy(request) {
63	  // Proxy logic
64	}
65	```
66	
67	### Config object (optional)
68	
69	Optionally, a config object can be exported alongside the Proxy function. This object includes the [matcher](#matcher) to specify paths where the Proxy applies.
70	
71	### Matcher
72	
73	The `matcher` option allows you to target specific paths for the Proxy to run on.
74	
75	Without a `matcher`, Proxy runs on **every request**, including static files (`_next/static`), image optimizations (`_next/image`), and assets in the `public/` folder. Consider using a [negative match pattern](#negative-matching) to exclude these paths, otherwise auth logic or redirects can unintentionally block CSS, JS, or images from loading.
76	
77	You can specify paths in several ways:
78	
79	- For a single path: Directly use a string to define the path, like `'/about'`.
80	- For multiple paths: Use an array to list multiple paths, such as `matcher: ['/about', '/contact']`, which applies the Proxy to both `/about` and `/contact`.
81	
82	```js filename="proxy.js"
83	export const config = {
84	  matcher: ['/about/:path*', '/dashboard/:path*'],
85	}
86	```
87	
88	Additionally, the `matcher` option supports complex path specifications using regular expressions. For example, you can exclude certain paths with a regular expression matcher:
89	
90	```js filename="proxy.js"
91	export const config = {
92	  matcher: [
93	    // Exclude API routes, static files, image optimizations, and .png files
94	    '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|.*\\.png$).*)',
95	  ],
96	}
97	```
98	
99	This enables precise control over which paths to include or exclude.
100	
101	The `matcher` option accepts an array of objects with the following keys:
102	
103	- `source`: The path or pattern used to match the request paths. It can be a string for direct path matching or a pattern for more complex matching.
104	- `locale` (optional): A boolean that, when set to `false`, ignores locale-based routing in path matching.
105	- `has` (optional): Specifies conditions based on the presence of specific request elements such as headers, query parameters, or cookies.
106	- `missing` (optional): Focuses on conditions where certain request elements are absent, like missing headers or cookies.
107	
108	```js filename="proxy.js"
109	export const config = {
110	  matcher: [
111	    {
112	      source: '/api/:path*',
113	      locale: false,
114	      has: [
115	        { type: 'header', key: 'Authorization', value: 'Bearer Token' },
116	        { type: 'query', key: 'userId', value: '123' },
117	      ],
118	      missing: [{ type: 'cookie', key: 'session', value: 'active' }],
119	    },
120	  ],
121	}
122	```
123	
124	The `source` path patterns:
125	
126	1. MUST start with `/`
127	2. Can include named parameters: `/about/:path` matches `/about/a` and `/about/b` but not `/about/a/c`
128	3. Can have modifiers on named parameters (starting with `:`): `/about/:path*` matches `/about/a/b/c` because `*` is _zero or more_. `?` is _zero or one_ and `+` _one or more_
129	4. Can use regular expression enclosed in parenthesis: `/about/(.*)` is the same as `/about/:path*`
130	5. Are anchored to the start of the path: `/about` matches `/about` and `/about/team` but not `/blog/about`
131	
132	Read more details on [path-to-regexp](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp#path-to-regexp-1) documentation.
133	
134	> **Good to know**:
135	>
136	> - The `matcher` values need to be constants so they can be statically analyzed at build-time. Dynamic values such as variables will be ignored.
137	> - For backward compatibility, Next.js always considers `/public` as `/public/index`. Therefore, a matcher of `/public/:path` will match.
138	
139	## Params
140	
141	Next.js calls the Proxy function with two arguments, [`request`](#request) and [`event`](#event), in that order. Declare only the ones you use.
142	
143	### `request`
144	
145	The first parameter is an instance of `NextRequest`, which represents the incoming HTTP request.
146	
147	```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
148	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
149	
150	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
151	  // Proxy logic goes here
152	}
153	```
154	
155	```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
156	export function proxy(request) {
157	  // Proxy logic goes here
158	}
159	```
160	
161	### `event`
162	
163	The second parameter is an instance of `NextFetchEvent`. It exposes a single method, `waitUntil(promise)`, which keeps the Proxy invocation alive until the promise settles, so background work like logging or analytics can finish after the response is sent. See [`waitUntil` and `NextFetchEvent`](#waituntil-and-nextfetchevent) for a full example.
164	
165	```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
166	import type { NextFetchEvent, NextRequest } from 'next/server'
167	
168	export function proxy(request: NextRequest, event: NextFetchEvent) {
169	  event.waitUntil(
170	    fetch('https://example.com/log', {
171	      method: 'POST',
172	      body: JSON.stringify({ pathname: request.nextUrl.pathname }),
173	    })
174	  )
175	}
176	```
177	
178	```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
179	export function proxy(request, event) {
180	  event.waitUntil(
181	    fetch('https://example.com/log', {
182	      method: 'POST',
183	      body: JSON.stringify({ pathname: request.nextUrl.pathname }),
184	    })
185	  )
186	}
187	```
188	
189	### `NextProxy` type
190	
191	If you prefer a shorthand, you can use the `NextProxy` type. It infers the parameter types for both `request` (`NextRequest`) and `event` (`NextFetchEvent`) automatically:
192	
193	```tsx filename="proxy.ts"
194	import type { NextProxy } from 'next/server'
195	
196	export const proxy: NextProxy = (request, event) => {
197	  event.waitUntil(Promise.resolve())
198	  return Response.json({ pathname: request.nextUrl.pathname })
199	}
200	```
201	
202	> **Good to know**:
203	>
204	> - `NextRequest` is a type that represents incoming HTTP requests in Next.js Proxy, whereas [`NextResponse`](#nextresponse) is a class used to manipulate and send back HTTP responses.

206	## NextResponse
207	
208	The `NextResponse` API allows you to:
209	
210	- `redirect` the incoming request to a different URL
211	- `rewrite` the response by displaying a given URL
212	- Set request headers for API Routes, `getServerSideProps`, and `rewrite` destinations
213	- Set response cookies
214	- Set response headers
215	
216	<AppOnly>
217	
218	To produce a response from Proxy, you can:
219	
220	1. `rewrite` to a route ([Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page) or [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route)) that produces a response
221	2. return a `NextResponse` directly. See [Producing a Response](#producing-a-response)
222	
223	> **Good to know**: For redirects, you can also use `Response.redirect` instead of `NextResponse.redirect`.
224	
225	</AppOnly>

227	<PagesOnly>
228	
229	To produce a response from Proxy, you can:
230	
231	1. `rewrite` to a route ([Page](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/pages-and-layouts) or [Edge API Route](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/api-routes)) that produces a response
232	2. return a `NextResponse` directly. See [Producing a Response](#producing-a-response)

236	## Execution order
237	
238	Proxy will be invoked for **every route in your project**. Given this, it's crucial to use [matchers](#matcher) to precisely target or exclude specific routes. The following is the execution order:
239	
240	1. `headers` from `next.config.js`
241	2. `redirects` from `next.config.js`
242	3. Proxy (`rewrites`, `redirects`, etc.)
243	4. `beforeFiles` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
244	5. Filesystem routes (`public/`, `_next/static/`, `pages/`, `app/`, etc.)
245	6. `afterFiles` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
246	7. Dynamic Routes (`/blog/[slug]`)
247	8. `fallback` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
248	
249	> **Good to know:** [Server Functions](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-server) are not separate routes in this chain. They are handled as POST requests to the route where they are used, so a Proxy matcher that excludes a path will also skip Server Function calls on that path.
250	>
251	> A matcher change or a refactor that moves a Server Function to a different route can silently remove Proxy coverage. Always verify authentication and authorization inside each Server Function rather than relying on Proxy alone. See the [Data Security guide](/docs/app/guides/data-security#authentication-and-authorization) for recommended patterns.
252	
253	## Runtime
254	
255	Proxy defaults to using the Node.js runtime. The [`runtime`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/runtime) config option is not available in Proxy files. Setting the `runtime` config option in Proxy will throw an error.
256	
257	## Advanced Proxy flags
258	
259	In `v13.1` of Next.js two additional flags were introduced for proxy, [`skipProxyUrlNormalize`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/skipProxyUrlNormalize) (formerly `skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize`) and [`skipTrailingSlashRedirect`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/skipTrailingSlashRedirect) to handle advanced use cases.
260	
261	`skipTrailingSlashRedirect` disables Next.js redirects for adding or removing trailing slashes. This allows custom handling inside proxy to maintain the trailing slash for some paths but not others, which can make incremental migrations easier.
262	
263	```js filename="next.config.js"
264	module.exports = {
265	  skipTrailingSlashRedirect: true,
266	}
267	```
268	
269	```js filename="proxy.js"
270	const legacyPrefixes = ['/docs', '/blog']
271	
272	export default async function proxy(req) {
273	  const { pathname } = req.nextUrl
274	
275	  if (legacyPrefixes.some((prefix) => pathname.startsWith(prefix))) {
276	    return NextResponse.next()
277	  }
278	
279	  // apply trailing slash handling
280	  if (
281	    !pathname.endsWith('/') &&
282	    !pathname.match(/((?!\.well-known(?:\/.*)?)(?:[^/]+\/)*[^/]+\.\w+)/)
283	  ) {
284	    return NextResponse.redirect(
285	      new URL(`${req.nextUrl.pathname}/`, req.nextUrl)
286	    )
287	  }
288	}
289	```
290	
291	`skipProxyUrlNormalize` allows for disabling the URL normalization in Next.js to make handling direct visits and client-transitions the same. In some advanced cases, this option provides full control by using the original URL.

344	### Using Cookies
345	
346	Cookies are regular headers. On a `Request`, they are stored in the `Cookie` header. On a `Response` they are in the `Set-Cookie` header. Next.js provides a convenient way to access and manipulate these cookies through the `cookies` extension on `NextRequest` and `NextResponse`.
347	
348	1. For incoming requests, `cookies` comes with the following methods: `get`, `getAll`, `set`, and `delete` cookies. You can check for the existence of a cookie with `has` or remove all cookies with `clear`.
349	2. For outgoing responses, `cookies` have the following methods `get`, `getAll`, `set`, and `delete`.
350	
351	```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
352	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
353	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
354	
355	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
356	  // Assume a "Cookie:nextjs=fast" header to be present on the incoming request
357	  // Getting cookies from the request using the `RequestCookies` API
358	  let cookie = request.cookies.get('nextjs')
359	  console.log(cookie) // => { name: 'nextjs', value: 'fast', Path: '/' }
360	  const allCookies = request.cookies.getAll()
361	  console.log(allCookies) // => [{ name: 'nextjs', value: 'fast' }]
362	
363	  request.cookies.has('nextjs') // => true
364	  request.cookies.delete('nextjs')
365	  request.cookies.has('nextjs') // => false
366	
367	  // Setting cookies on the response using the `ResponseCookies` API
368	  const response = NextResponse.next()
369	  response.cookies.set('vercel', 'fast')
370	  response.cookies.set({
371	    name: 'vercel',
372	    value: 'fast',
373	    path: '/',
374	  })
375	  cookie = response.cookies.get('vercel')
376	  console.log(cookie) // => { name: 'vercel', value: 'fast', Path: '/' }
377	  // The outgoing response will have a `Set-Cookie:vercel=fast;path=/` header.
378	
379	  return response
380	}
381	```

414	### Setting Headers
415	
416	You can set request and response headers using the `NextResponse` API (setting _request_ headers is available since Next.js v13.0.0).
417	
418	```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
419	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
420	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
421	
422	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
423	  // Clone the request headers and set a new header `x-hello-from-proxy1`
424	  const requestHeaders = new Headers(request.headers)
425	  requestHeaders.set('x-hello-from-proxy1', 'hello')
426	
427	  // You can also set request headers in NextResponse.next
428	  const response = NextResponse.next({
429	    request: {
430	      // New request headers
431	      headers: requestHeaders,
432	    },
433	  })
434	
435	  // Set a new response header `x-hello-from-proxy2`
436	  response.headers.set('x-hello-from-proxy2', 'hello')
437	  return response
438	}
439	```

472	#### RSC requests and rewrites
473	
474	During RSC requests, Next.js strips internal Flight headers from the `request` instance in Proxy. For example, headers like `rsc`, `next-router-state-tree`, and `next-router-prefetch` are not exposed through `request.headers`. This is to prevent accidentally handling an RSC request differently than the HTML request as both need to align.
475	
476	When you use `NextResponse.rewrite()`, Next.js automatically propagates the required RSC rewrite headers upstream.
477	
478	If you implement custom rewrite logic with `fetch()` instead of `NextResponse.rewrite()`, you can run into missing RSC headers unless you forward them manually.
479	
480	For custom `fetch` rewrite setups, you can also enable [`skipProxyUrlNormalize`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/skipProxyUrlNormalize) in `next.config.js` so your rewrite logic can receive the necessary URL shape and RSC headers from the provided request object:
481	
482	```js filename="next.config.js"
483	module.exports = {
484	  skipProxyUrlNormalize: true,
485	}
486	```

488	### CORS
489	
490	You can set CORS headers in Proxy to allow cross-origin requests, including [simple](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS#simple_requests) and [preflighted](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS#preflighted_requests) requests.
491	
492	```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
493	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
494	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
495	
496	const allowedOrigins = ['https://acme.com', 'https://my-app.org']
497	
498	const corsOptions = {
499	  'Access-Control-Allow-Methods': 'GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS',
500	  'Access-Control-Allow-Headers': 'Content-Type, Authorization',
501	}
502	
503	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
504	  // Check the origin from the request
505	  const origin = request.headers.get('origin') ?? ''
506	  const isAllowedOrigin = allowedOrigins.includes(origin)
507	
508	  // Handle preflighted requests
509	  const isPreflight = request.method === 'OPTIONS'
510	
511	  if (isPreflight) {
512	    const preflightHeaders = {
513	      ...(isAllowedOrigin && { 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': origin }),
514	      ...corsOptions,
515	    }
516	    return NextResponse.json({}, { headers: preflightHeaders })
517	  }
518	
519	  // Handle simple requests
520	  const response = NextResponse.next()
521	
522	  if (isAllowedOrigin) {
523	    response.headers.set('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', origin)
524	  }
525	
526	  Object.entries(corsOptions).forEach(([key, value]) => {
527	    response.headers.set(key, value)
528	  })
529	
530	  return response
531	}
532	
533	export const config = {
534	  matcher: '/api/:path*',
535	}
536	```

634	### Negative matching
635	
636	The `matcher` config allows full regex so matching like negative lookaheads or character matching is supported. An example of a negative lookahead to match all except specific paths can be seen here:
637	
638	```js filename="proxy.js"
639	export const config = {
640	  matcher: [
641	    /*
642	     * Match all request paths except for the ones starting with:
643	     * - api (API routes)
644	     * - _next/static (static files)
645	     * - _next/image (image optimization files)
646	     * - favicon.ico, sitemap.xml, robots.txt (metadata files)
647	     */
648	    '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
649	  ],
650	}
651	```
652	
653	You can also bypass Proxy for certain requests by using the `missing` or `has` arrays, or a combination of both:
654	
655	```js filename="proxy.js"
656	export const config = {
657	  matcher: [
658	    /*
659	     * Match all request paths except for the ones starting with:
660	     * - api (API routes)
661	     * - _next/static (static files)
662	     * - _next/image (image optimization files)
663	     * - favicon.ico, sitemap.xml, robots.txt (metadata files)
664	     */
665	    {
666	      source:
667	        '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
668	      missing: [
669	        { type: 'header', key: 'next-router-prefetch' },
670	        { type: 'header', key: 'purpose', value: 'prefetch' },
671	      ],
672	    },
673	
674	    {
675	      source:
676	        '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
677	      has: [
678	        { type: 'header', key: 'next-router-prefetch' },
679	        { type: 'header', key: 'purpose', value: 'prefetch' },
680	      ],
681	    },
682	
683	    {
684	      source:
685	        '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
686	      has: [{ type: 'header', key: 'x-present' }],
687	      missing: [{ type: 'header', key: 'x-missing', value: 'prefetch' }],
688	    },
689	  ],
690	}
691	```
692	
693	> **Good to know**:
694	>
695	> Even when `_next/data` is excluded in a negative matcher pattern, proxy will still be invoked for `_next/data` routes. This is intentional behavior to prevent accidental security issues where you might protect a page but forget to protect the corresponding data route.
696	
697	```js filename="proxy.js"
698	export const config = {
699	  matcher:
700	    '/((?!api|_next/data|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
701	}
702	
703	// Proxy will still run for /_next/data/* routes despite being excluded
704	```

706	### `waitUntil` and `NextFetchEvent`
707	
708	The `NextFetchEvent` object extends the native [`FetchEvent`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/FetchEvent) object, and includes the [`waitUntil()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/ExtendableEvent/waitUntil) method.
709	
710	The `waitUntil()` method takes a promise as an argument, and extends the lifetime of the Proxy until the promise settles. This is useful for performing work in the background.
711	
712	```ts filename="proxy.ts"
713	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
714	import type { NextFetchEvent, NextRequest } from 'next/server'
715	
716	export function proxy(req: NextRequest, event: NextFetchEvent) {
717	  event.waitUntil(
718	    fetch('https://my-analytics-platform.com', {
719	      method: 'POST',
720	      body: JSON.stringify({ pathname: req.nextUrl.pathname }),
721	    })
722	  )
723	
724	  return NextResponse.next()
725	}
726	```

728	### Unit testing (experimental)
729	
730	Starting in Next.js 15.1, the `next/experimental/testing/server` package contains utilities to help unit test proxy files. Unit testing proxy can help ensure that it's only run on desired paths and that custom routing logic works as intended before code reaches production.
731	
732	The `unstable_doesProxyMatch` function can be used to assert whether proxy will run for the provided URL, headers, and cookies.
733	
734	```js
735	import { unstable_doesProxyMatch } from 'next/experimental/testing/server'
736	
737	expect(
738	  unstable_doesProxyMatch({
739	    config,
740	    nextConfig,
741	    url: '/test',
742	  })
743	).toEqual(false)
744	```
745	
746	The entire proxy function can also be tested.
747	
748	```js
749	import { isRewrite, getRewrittenUrl } from 'next/experimental/testing/server'
750	
751	const request = new NextRequest('https://nextjs.org/docs')
752	const response = await proxy(request)
753	expect(isRewrite(response)).toEqual(true)
754	expect(getRewrittenUrl(response)).toEqual('https://other-domain.com/docs')
755	// getRedirectUrl could also be used if the response were a redirect
756	```

769	## Migration to Proxy
770	
771	### Why the Change
772	
773	The reason behind the renaming of `middleware` is that the term "middleware" can often be confused with Express.js middleware, leading to a misinterpretation of its purpose. Also, Middleware is highly capable, so it may encourage the usage; however, this feature is recommended to be used as a last resort.
774	
775	Next.js is moving forward to provide better APIs with better ergonomics so that developers can achieve their goals without Middleware. This is the reason behind the renaming of `middleware`.
776	
777	### Why "Proxy"
778	
779	The name Proxy clarifies what Middleware is capable of. The term "proxy" implies a network boundary in front of the app, which is how this feature behaves. It can run outside of your application’s main runtime and handle requests before they reach your app. These characteristics align better with the term "proxy" and provide a clearer purpose for the feature.
780	
781	### How to Migrate
782	
783	We recommend users avoid relying on Middleware unless no other options exist. Our goal is to give them APIs with better ergonomics so they can achieve their goals without Middleware.
784	
785	The term “middleware” often confuses users with Express.js middleware, which can encourage misuse. To clarify our direction, we are renaming the file convention to “proxy.” This highlights that we are moving away from Middleware, breaking down its overloaded features, and making the Proxy clear in its purpose.
786	
787	Next.js provides a codemod to migrate from `middleware.ts` to `proxy.ts`. You can run the following command to migrate:
788	
789	```bash
790	npx @next/codemod@canary middleware-to-proxy .
791	```
792	
793	The codemod will rename the file and the function name from `middleware` to `proxy`.
794	
795	```diff
796	// middleware.ts -> proxy.ts
797	
798	- export function middleware() {
799	+ export function proxy() {
800	```

---
title: How to set up instrumentation
nav_title: Instrumentation
description: Learn how to use instrumentation to run code at server startup in your Next.js app
related:
  title: Learn more about Instrumentation
  links:

{/* The content of this doc is shared between the app and pages router. You can use the `<PagesOnly>Content</PagesOnly>` component to add content that is specific to the Pages Router. Any shared content should not be wrapped in a component. */}
Instrumentation is the process of using code to integrate monitoring and logging tools into your application. This allows you to track the performance and behavior of your application, and to debug issues in production.
## Convention
To set up instrumentation, create `instrumentation.ts|js` file in the **root directory** of your project (or inside the [`src`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/src-folder) folder if using one).
Then, export a `register` function in the file. This function will be called **once** when a new Next.js server instance is initiated, and must complete before the server is ready to handle requests.
For example, to use Next.js with [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/) and [@vercel/otel](https://vercel.com/docs/tracing/instrumentation):
```ts filename="instrumentation.ts" switcher
import { registerOTel } from '@vercel/otel'
export function register() {
  registerOTel('next-app')
}
```
```js filename="instrumentation.js" switcher
import { registerOTel } from '@vercel/otel'
export function register() {
  registerOTel('next-app')
}
```
See the [Next.js with OpenTelemetry example](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/with-opentelemetry) for a complete implementation.
> **Good to know**:
>
> - The `instrumentation` file should be in the root of your project and not inside the `app` or `pages` directory. If you're using the `src` folder, then place the file inside `src` alongside `pages` and `app`.
> - If you use the [`pageExtensions` config option](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/pageExtensions) to add a suffix, you will also need to update the `instrumentation` filename to match.
## Examples
### Importing files with side effects
Sometimes, it may be useful to import a file in your code because of the side effects it will cause. For example, you might import a file that defines a set of global variables, but never explicitly use the imported file in your code. You would still have access to the global variables the package has declared.
We recommend importing files using JavaScript `import` syntax within your `register` function. The following example demonstrates a basic usage of `import` in a `register` function:
```ts filename="instrumentation.ts" switcher
export async function register() {
  await import('package-with-side-effect')
}
```
```js filename="instrumentation.js" switcher
export async function register() {
  await import('package-with-side-effect')
}
```
> **Good to know:**
>
> We recommend importing the file from within the `register` function, rather than at the top of the file. By doing this, you can colocate all of your side effects in one place in your code, and avoid any unintended consequences from importing globally at the top of the file.
### Importing runtime-specific code
Next.js calls `register` in all environments, so it's important to conditionally import any code that doesn't support specific runtimes (e.g. [Edge or Node.js](/docs/app/api-reference/edge)). You can use the `NEXT_RUNTIME` environment variable to get the current environment:
```ts filename="instrumentation.ts" switcher
export async function register() {
  if (process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME === 'nodejs') {
    await import('./instrumentation-node')
  }
  if (process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME === 'edge') {
    await import('./instrumentation-edge')
  }
}
